title: The DOJ Is Weighing Perjury Charges Against Cassidy Hutchinson
gist: Federal prosecutors are weighing perjury and obstruction charges against Cassidy Hutchinson over inconsistencies between her January 6 committee testimony and her account to Jack Smith's team, but are not expected to seek an indictment until after the midterms. The referral landed in the DOJ Civil Rights Division under Harmeet Dhillon, and some Justice officials doubt a viable case exists.

insights.claim: DOJ prosecutors are weighing perjury and obstruction-of-justice charges against Cassidy Hutchinson, the former Meadows aide who implicated Trump in her January 6 committee testimony.
insights.speaker: Hugo Lowell
insights.so_what: Signals the DOJ is actively pursuing a politically sensitive prosecution; watch for grand jury activity.

insights.claim: Prosecutors are not expected to ask a Washington grand jury for an indictment until at least after the midterm elections.
insights.speaker: Hugo Lowell
insights.so_what: Timing pushes any charging decision past the midterms, so event risk sits in late 2026 or later.

insights.claim: Prosecutors are building the case by comparing transcripts of Hutchinson's committee interviews against her testimony to Jack Smith's team, focusing on how her account changed and on Smith's failure to corroborate much of it.
insights.speaker: Hugo Lowell
insights.so_what: The case rests on testimonial inconsistencies, a weaker basis than documentary evidence.

insights.claim: Prosecutors have focused on Hutchinson's claim that she wrote a notecard statement for Trump to release during the riot, which former White House counsel Eric Herschmann disputes, saying he wrote the note.
insights.speaker: Hugo Lowell
insights.so_what: Shows the specific disputed factual claims that could anchor a perjury theory.

insights.claim: Some Justice officials doubt there is a viable criminal case against Hutchinson, partly because of the high bar for proving perjury.
insights.speaker: Hugo Lowell
insights.so_what: Raises odds that the matter stalls or is dropped despite political pressure.

insights.claim: To convict on perjury, prosecutors must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Hutchinson lied, did so knowingly, and that it materially affected the investigation.
insights.speaker: Joyce Vance
insights.so_what: Three-part standard is demanding, making conviction hard on inconsistency alone.

insights.claim: The investigation became a DOJ priority after a criminal referral by Rep. Barry Loudermilk, a longtime critic of the January 6 committee.

insights.claim: The referral was unorthodoxly assigned to the Civil Rights Division led by Trump loyalist Harmeet Dhillon rather than the DC US Attorney or Criminal Division, though that division is supposed to take only cases with a civil rights nexus.
insights.speaker: Hugo Lowell
insights.so_what: Irregular venue choice suggests the process is driven by political alignment and invites legal challenge.

insights.claim: The grand jury probe is the latest example of the DOJ pursuing criminal cases against Trump's perceived political enemies, and Trump fired AG Pam Bondi in April partly for moving too slowly on such cases.
